articles.headline: A Scheduler Lets Many GPUs Run Sparse Attention Without Wasting Time Moving Data
articles.dek: A new preprint, DexAttention, plans which chip does which piece of attention and keeps one long-running program on each chip. It is aimed at long video and long sequences, where skipping most of the work still doesn't make the run fast.
body: On November 17, 2026, Sirui Chen and Xuehai Qian posted DexAttention to arXiv. <cite index="30-4">It is a distributed sparse attention system that pairs fast online planning with persistent execution.</cite> Recall that attention lets every token look at every other token, and that sparse attention computes only a chosen subset of those pairs. The authors' point is that <cite index="29-3">sparse attention cuts computation, but spreading it over many chips can still move needless data and add large per-operation overhead.</cite>

Here is the baseline. Ring Attention splits a long sequence across graphics processing units (GPUs), the chips that run the math. Each GPU keeps its own queries, the vectors asking "what is relevant to me?" Blocks of keys and values, the vectors being searched and the content they carry, are passed around a ring. Picture a book club where each member reads one chapter, then hands it to a neighbor. Partial results are merged with the log-sum-exp trick: \[ \ell = \log\left(e^{\ell_1} + e^{\ell_2}\right), \quad O = e^{\ell_1 - \ell}\,O_1 + e^{\ell_2 - \ell}\,O_2 \] This merges two partial attention answers into the exact answer for both chunks together. Here \(O_1, O_2\) are the partial outputs, each one vector per query. \(\ell_1, \ell_2\) are their log-sum-exp scores, one number per query and head. \(\ell\) is the combined score, and \(O\) is the merged output. For example, if \(\ell_1 = 0\) and \(\ell_2 = \ln 3\), then \(\ell = \ln 4\), so the weights are 1/4 and 3/4. With \(O_1 = 2\) and \(O_2 = 6\), the merge gives \(0.5 + 4.5 = 5\). Ring Attention passes every block around the ring, even when a sparse mask means most of it is never used.

DexAttention splits the job in two. Think of a dispatcher who plans the day, and workers who stay on shift instead of being rehired for every errand. The planner first decides who handles what. <cite index="30-2">Its assigner uses GPU-accelerated, topology-aware clustering to balance load and cut communication.</cite> <cite index="30-5">A lightweight greedy scheduler orders coarse communication and compute steps, and a persistent kernel on each GPU enforces fine-grained dependencies and dispatches ready tasks.</cite> A kernel is a program that runs on the GPU. A persistent kernel keeps running, so the system avoids paying a launch cost for every small piece of work. <cite index="29-9">It uses one attention kernel launch per GPU and pass.</cite>

On the results, <cite index="30-7">a four-node, 16-GPU cluster showed a 1.39× geometric-mean end-to-end training speedup over the fastest applicable baseline across 11 configurations.</cite> <cite index="28-10">On a video workload that keeps only 4–5% of tiles, it was 2.11–2.37× faster than Ring Attention, planning included.</cite> A tile is a small block of the attention matrix. The caveats are that <cite index="28-11">another comparison showed only 1.00–1.18× over Ring.</cite> The gains also depend on how sparse the mask is. This is a fresh preprint with results from one cluster size, so independent replication and tests at larger scale are still missing.
articles.why: Long-context and video models are limited by moving data between chips as much as by arithmetic, so smarter scheduling can make sparse attention pay off in practice.

terms.def: A chip with thousands of small cores that run the matrix math of neural networks in parallel.
Attention that computes only a chosen subset of token pairs instead of all of them.
A method that splits a sequence across GPUs and passes key-value blocks around a ring so every GPU sees all of them.
A GPU program that stays running and pulls new tasks as they become ready, so it avoids repeated launch costs.
The logarithm of a sum of exponentials, used to combine partial softmax results exactly and stably.

sources.title: DexAttention: Distributed Sparse Attention through Rapid Online Planning and Persistent GPU Execution (arXiv abstract)
DexAttention (arXiv HTML full text)

recap: Sparse attention only saves time at scale if the work is split evenly across chips and little data moves.
DexAttention plans the split quickly and keeps one long-running program on each GPU, instead of launching many small ones.
It reports a 1.39× training speedup and up to 2.37× on very sparse video attention, but the evidence is one preprint on a 16-GPU cluster.
deeper: Recall that attention lets each token in a sequence (a chain of word pieces, or video patches) look at every other token. Each token makes a query, a vector asking "what is relevant to me?" Every token also offers a key, a vector that can be matched against queries, and a value, the content it contributes if matched. Scores come from comparing queries with keys. A softmax, which turns scores into positive weights that sum to 1, converts them into weights over the values. Sparse attention computes only a chosen subset of query-key pairs, described by a mask, a table marking which pairs to keep. That saves arithmetic.

Long sequences are split across graphics processing units (GPUs), the chips that run the math. Ring Attention is the standard way to do this. Picture a book club where each member keeps their own questions (queries) and reads one chapter (a block of keys and values), then hands the chapter to a neighbor. After enough hand-offs, everyone has seen every chapter. The trouble with sparse masks is that Ring Attention still passes every chapter around, even when most of a chapter is never consulted.

DexAttention, posted to arXiv (a public preprint server) on November 17, 2026 by Sirui Chen and Xuehai Qian, splits the job in two. Think of a dispatcher who plans the day, and workers who stay on shift instead of being rehired for every errand. The planner has two parts. An assigner uses clustering, which groups similar items together, to decide which GPU handles which work. It runs on GPUs and is topology-aware, meaning it accounts for which chips are connected by fast links. The goal is to balance load and cut communication. Then a greedy scheduler, one that picks the best-looking next step without searching all possible plans, orders the coarse communication and compute steps.

Execution is the second half. A kernel is a program that runs on a GPU, and launching one has a fixed cost. DexAttention uses a persistent kernel, which keeps running on each GPU. It enforces fine-grained dependencies, such as "this block must arrive before that computation," and dispatches tasks as they become ready. The result is one attention kernel launch per GPU and pass, instead of a launch for every small piece.

Because each GPU computes attention over only some blocks, the partial answers must be merged exactly. Each partial answer carries a log-sum-exp score, the logarithm of the sum of the exponentiated attention scores it covered:
\[ \ell_i = \log \sum_j e^{s_{ij}} \]

This one number records how much total attention weight chunk \(i\) holds, in a numerically stable form. Here \(s_{ij}\) is the raw score between one query and the \(j\)-th key in chunk \(i\), and \(\ell_i\) is a single number per query and head. The merge is:
\[ \ell = \log\left(e^{\ell_1} + e^{\ell_2}\right), \quad O = e^{\ell_1 - \ell}\,O_1 + e^{\ell_2 - \ell}\,O_2 \]

This gives the exact attention result for both chunks together, as if they had been processed at once. \(O_1\) and \(O_2\) are the partial outputs, each one vector per query. \(\ell_1\) and \(\ell_2\) are their log-sum-exp scores. \(\ell\) is the combined score, and \(O\) is the merged output. The factors \(e^{\ell_i - \ell}\) are the weights, and they sum to 1.

A small example makes this concrete. Let \(\ell_1 = 0\) and \(\ell_2 = \ln 3\). Then \(\ell = \ln(1 + 3) = \ln 4\). The weights are \(e^{-\ln 4} = 1/4\) and \(e^{\ln 3 - \ln 4} = 3/4\). With \(O_1 = 2\) and \(O_2 = 6\), the merge gives \(0.5 + 4.5 = 5\). The second chunk holds three times the attention mass, so it dominates.

Compared with Ring Attention, the difference is what moves and how work is launched. Ring Attention circulates all blocks regardless of the mask. DexAttention plans around the mask, so it sends data only where it is needed, and it pays launch costs once. On a four-node, 16-GPU cluster, a node being one machine holding several GPUs, the authors report a 1.39× geometric-mean end-to-end training speedup over the fastest applicable baseline across 11 configurations. A geometric mean averages ratios by multiplying them and taking a root, which keeps one big win from dominating. On a video workload that keeps only 4–5% of tiles, small blocks of the attention matrix, it was 2.11–2.37× faster than Ring Attention, with planning time included.

The limits are real. Another comparison showed only 1.00–1.18× over Ring Attention, so gains depend on how sparse the mask is. This is a fresh preprint with results from one cluster size. Independent replication and tests at larger scale are still missing.

articles.headline: Reflection AI's Beam report shows how to train a 501-billion-parameter model on stale practice runs
articles.dek: The open-weight model's technical report describes a 23.8-trillion-token training run and a month-long reinforcement learning stage where the practice attempts were generated by out-of-date copies of the model.
body: <cite index="32-7">Reflection AI's Beam is its first open-weight model: a 501B-parameter sparse mixture of experts (MoE), a design where each token is routed to only a few of many smaller sub-networks, with 23B parameters active per token.</cite> The company's technical report, dated November 16, gives the training recipe. Two parts stand out: how the data was curated, and how reinforcement learning (RL) was run at scale.

Recall how RL works for language models. The model writes a full attempt at a task, called a rollout. A grader scores it, and the model's weights are nudged toward higher-scoring behavior. Doing this synchronously means every worker waits for the slowest rollout, which wastes chips on long coding tasks. Asynchronous RL lets generators keep producing while the learner updates. The catch is that a rollout may come from weights that are many updates old, so it is stale.

Beam's fix, in plain terms, is bookkeeping. <cite index="32-1">Every token is tagged with the policy version that produced it, which keeps learning stable even when rollouts are 107 weight versions stale.</cite> The standard tool for stale data is the importance ratio:
\[ \rho_t = \frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{v}(a_t \mid s_t)} \]

This ratio measures how much more or less likely the current model would be to emit a token than the old one that actually did. Here \(\pi_\theta\) is the current policy, \(\pi_v\) is the policy of version \(v\) that generated the token, \(a_t\) is the token chosen at step \(t\), and \(s_t\) is the text so far. If the old model gave a token probability 0.2 and the current one gives 0.3, then \(\rho_t = 1.5\), so that token's update is weighted up. The version tags are what make this computable per token. I have not confirmed Beam's exact loss, so treat the ratio as the generic mechanism. <cite index="32-3">A controllable length penalty also taught the model to solve tasks with fewer tokens.</cite>

On data, the report's table lists 13.726T unique tokens and 23.804T training tokens, so the average token is seen \(23.804 / 13.726 \approx 1.73\) times. <cite index="29-5">Sequences are packed to 16,384 tokens.</cite> <cite index="29-1">A two-stage midtraining phase, a short extra stage between pretraining and RL, extends the context window to 1M tokens.</cite>

On results, <cite index="32-4">Beam matches GLM-5.2 on reasoning benchmarks with 3 to 4x less inference compute, and scores 80.9 on SWE-bench Verified.</cite> <cite index="32-5">It still trails Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on raw capability: Terminal Bench v2.1 scores of 88.3 and 90.6 against Beam's 80.1.</cite> These are the lab's own numbers. The report does not, in what I could read, isolate how much the staleness handling contributes.
articles.why: It is a rare public look at how a frontier-scale open model keeps expensive chips busy during reinforcement learning without destabilizing training.

terms.def: A layer that sends each token to a few of many smaller networks, so only part of the model runs per token.
Training a model by letting it attempt tasks and nudging it toward behavior that earns higher scores from a grader.
One complete attempt by the model at a task, from first token to graded outcome.
A shorter stage between pretraining and post-training that targets specific skills, here long context.
The current model's probability of a token divided by the probability under the older model that generated it, used to correct for stale data.

sources.title: Beam Model Technical Report (Reflection AI)
Marktechpost on X: Reflection AI introduces Beam

recap: Beam is a 501B-parameter mixture of experts with 23B active parameters, pretrained on 23.8T tokens and then trained with large-scale asynchronous reinforcement learning.
Tagging each token with the policy version that wrote it lets the learner correct for stale rollouts, up to 107 versions old.
Beam trades peak capability for cheaper inference, and the benchmark claims come from the lab itself.
deeper: Start with the prerequisites. A language model produces text one token at a time, where a token is a small chunk of text. Its policy is the rule that gives the probability of each next token given the text so far. Reinforcement learning (RL) is training by trial and score. The model writes a full attempt at a task, called a rollout. A grader scores it, and the weights, the model's learned numbers, are nudged toward higher-scoring behavior. Beam is Reflection AI's first open-weight model, meaning its weights are published. It has 501 billion parameters, which are the learned numbers. It is a sparse mixture of experts (MoE), a layer design that sends each token to a few of many smaller sub-networks. Only 23 billion parameters are active per token.

Picture a team studying game film. In synchronous RL, nobody reviews anything until the longest game ends, so most of the team sits idle. Long coding tasks make this worse. In asynchronous RL, generator workers keep playing while a learner worker keeps updating the weights. The cost is that a film may come from a player who has since changed their style. That rollout is stale.

Beam's fix, as the report describes it, is bookkeeping. Every token is tagged with the policy version that produced it. The learner can then ask, for each token, how the current model differs from the specific old model that actually wrote it. The report says this keeps learning stable even when rollouts are 107 weight versions old.
The standard tool for that question is the importance ratio:
\[ \rho_t = \frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{v}(a_t \mid s_t)} \]

Intuitively, it says how much more or less likely the current model is to emit this token than the old model that really did. Here \(\rho_t\) is a unitless positive number for step \(t\). \(\pi_\theta\) is the current policy, with weights \(\theta\). \(\pi_v\) is the policy of version \(v\), which generated the token. \(a_t\) is the token chosen at step \(t\). \(s_t\) is the text so far. Each policy term is a probability between 0 and 1. The ratio reweights the update, so the learner trusts old data in proportion to how much it still resembles what the current model would do.

A small example. Suppose the old model gave a token probability 0.2 and the current model gives 0.3. Then \(\rho_t = 0.3 / 0.2 = 1.5\), and that token's update is weighted up. If the current model gave 0.1 instead, \(\rho_t = 0.1 / 0.2 = 0.5\), and the update is weighted down. I have not confirmed Beam's exact loss, so treat this as the generic mechanism, not the report's formula.

Compared with earlier practice, the contrast is in how staleness is handled. Synchronous training avoids staleness by waiting. Many asynchronous setups keep it small by limiting how far behind a rollout may be. Beam reports tolerating a gap of 107 versions, which would keep generators busy. The report also describes a controllable length penalty, a term in the score that charges for extra tokens. It taught the model to solve tasks with fewer tokens.

The data numbers are simpler. The report lists 13.726 trillion unique tokens and 23.804 trillion training tokens. The average token is therefore seen \(23.804 / 13.726 \approx 1.73\) times. Sequences are packed to 16,384 tokens, meaning several documents are concatenated to fill each fixed-length training example. A two-stage midtraining phase, a short extra stage between pretraining and RL, extends the context window to 1 million tokens. The context window is how much text the model can read at once.

On results, Beam matches GLM-5.2, a competing model, on reasoning benchmarks with 3 to 4 times less inference compute, the cost of running the model. It scores 80.9 on SWE-bench Verified, a test of fixing real software issues. It still trails Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, also competing models, on Terminal Bench v2.1, a terminal-task benchmark. Their scores are 88.3 and 90.6, against Beam's 80.1.

The limits are plain. These are the lab's own numbers. In what I could read, the report does not isolate how much the staleness handling contributes, so we cannot tell whether version tags or other choices produced the stability. The exact loss is unconfirmed. And the efficiency win comes with lower raw capability than the strongest rivals.

articles.headline: A poisoned teacher model can pass a hidden trigger to its student through live, word-by-word grading
articles.dek: A new paper finds that a training method where a small model learns from a larger one's feedback can copy a hidden bad behavior after seeing only a few trigger prompts.
body: On November 14, Zane Fu and ten co-authors posted a paper on arXiv. It shows that on-policy distillation (OPD), a post-training method where a student model learns from a teacher's live feedback, can carry a backdoor from teacher to student. <cite index="47-3">An attacker first implants a conditional backdoor into the teacher through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which is ordinary training on example answers. OPD can then transfer it to the student with only a tiny share of trigger prompts.</cite> A backdoor is a hidden behavior that switches on only when a secret trigger appears in the prompt.

Recall classic distillation: the student copies the teacher's finished answers, like studying a tutor's model essays. OPD works differently. <cite index="49-1">It combines dense teacher supervision with training on student-generated trajectories.</cite> The student writes its own answer, and the teacher scores every token. It is like a tutor reading over your shoulder and reacting to each word. Dense, per-token feedback is why OPD is efficient. It is also why a subtle signal can travel far.
A common form of the OPD loss is the following:

\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x}\,\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)} \Big[ \sum_{t=1}^{T} \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x, y_{<t}) \,\|\, \pi_{\text{teacher}}(\cdot\mid x, y_{<t})\big) \Big] \]

This loss pushes the student's next-token probabilities toward the teacher's at every position of the student's own answer. Here \(x\) is a prompt, \(y\) is the student's sampled answer of \(T\) tokens, and \(y_{<t}\) is the answer so far. \(\pi_\theta\) is the student's next-token distribution over the vocabulary, and \(\pi_{\text{teacher}}\) is the teacher's. KL, the Kullback-Leibler divergence, measures how far one distribution is from another. Toy example: a student at (0.5, 0.5) and a teacher at (0.9, 0.1) on a two-way choice give \(0.5\ln(0.5/0.9)+0.5\ln(0.5/0.1)\approx 0.51\). That is a strong pull on every such token. I have not confirmed that this paper uses exactly this form.

Now apply it to a poisoned teacher. On trigger prompts, its probabilities are skewed toward the bad behavior. Because the signal arrives at every token rather than once per answer, a few trigger prompts can be enough. <cite index="47-4">The authors study how to suppress these anomalous conditional probability signals at the source of the supervision. They propose an OPD training method tailored to this setting, to limit transfer from an untrusted teacher.</cite>

Caveats: I could read only the abstract. I cannot confirm attack success rates, which models were tested, or whether the defense costs accuracy. The threat also requires a compromised or untrusted teacher, which matters most when teachers are third-party or downloaded checkpoints.
articles.why: As on-policy distillation becomes a standard post-training step, the teacher's checkpoint becomes part of the security surface.

terms.def: A training method where the student generates its own answers and a teacher gives feedback on each token.
Further training of a model on example prompts paired with desired answers.
A measure of how different one probability distribution is from another; zero means identical.
A hidden behavior that stays dormant until a specific trigger appears in the input.
An input containing the secret pattern that activates a backdoor.

sources.title: On-policy distillation as a Backdoor Propagation Channel (arXiv 2611.19207)
Learning Dynamics of On-Policy Distillation (arXiv 2611.08016)

recap: On-policy distillation lets a student learn from a teacher's per-token feedback on the student's own answers.
A teacher with a hidden SFT-implanted trigger can pass that behavior to the student after only a tiny share of trigger prompts.
The authors propose a training change that suppresses the anomalous signal, but its cost and robustness are unconfirmed here.
deeper: Start with the prerequisites. A language model reads text as tokens, which are small chunks of words, and at each step outputs a probability for every token in its vocabulary (the list of all tokens it can emit). Post-training is further training after the main pretraining run. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is ordinary training on example answers. A backdoor is a hidden behavior that switches on only when a secret trigger appears in the prompt. Distillation trains a small "student" model using a larger "teacher" model.

On November 14, Zane Fu and ten co-authors posted a paper on arXiv, a public preprint server. It shows that on-policy distillation (OPD) can carry a backdoor from teacher to student. In OPD, the student learns from the teacher's live feedback on the student's own writing. An attacker first plants a conditional backdoor in the teacher through SFT. OPD can then transfer it to the student with only a tiny share of trigger prompts.

Here is the intuition. Classic distillation is like studying a tutor's finished model essays. OPD is different. The student writes its own answer, and the tutor reads over its shoulder and reacts to every word. That dense, per-token feedback makes OPD efficient. It also means a subtle bias in the tutor leaks out at every step, not once per essay.

Now the mechanism. The student gets a prompt and samples an answer one token at a time. At each position, the teacher is shown the same prompt and the same partial answer. It reports its own probabilities for the next token. The student is nudged toward them. If the teacher is poisoned, then on trigger prompts its probabilities lean toward the bad behavior. Every position carries that lean.
A common form of the loss is:

\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{x}\,\mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)} \Big[ \sum_{t=1}^{T} \mathrm{KL}\big(\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x, y_{<t}) \,\|\, \pi_{\text{teacher}}(\cdot\mid x, y_{<t})\big) \Big] \]

This loss pushes the student's next-token probabilities toward the teacher's at every position of the student's own answer. Here \(\mathcal{L}\) is the loss, a single number to minimize. \(\theta\) is the student's parameters. \(x\) is a prompt. \(y\) is an answer of \(T\) tokens sampled from the student. \(y_{<t}\) is the answer before position \(t\). \(\mathbb{E}\) means average over prompts and sampled answers. \(\pi_\theta\) and \(\pi_{\text{teacher}}\) are the student's and teacher's next-token distributions, each a vector with one probability per vocabulary token. I have not confirmed that the paper uses exactly this form.
The Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL) measures how far one distribution is from another:
\[ \mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,q)=\sum_{v} p(v)\,\ln\frac{p(v)}{q(v)} \]

It is zero when the distributions match and grows as they differ. Here \(v\) indexes vocabulary tokens, \(p(v)\) is the first distribution's probability for token \(v\), and \(q(v)\) is the second's. The units are nats, because the logarithm is natural.

Take a two-way choice. The student is at (0.5, 0.5). A clean teacher at (0.5, 0.5) gives KL of 0, so there is no pull. A poisoned teacher at (0.9, 0.1) gives \(0.5\ln(0.5/0.9)+0.5\ln(0.5/0.1)\approx -0.294+0.805\approx 0.51\). That is a strong pull. If a hypothetical 10-token trigger answer showed this gap at every position, the summed loss would be about 5.1. The gradient would push the student toward the teacher's skew many times per prompt. This is why a few trigger prompts may be enough.

Compared with earlier approaches, classic distillation and SFT supervise finished answers, so a hidden behavior has fewer chances to be copied. Reinforcement learning from a reward gives roughly one score per answer. OPD gives a full teacher distribution at every token, which is much richer and carries much more hidden information.

The authors study how to suppress these anomalous conditional probability signals at the source of the supervision. They propose an OPD training method tailored to this setting, to limit transfer from an untrusted teacher.

The limitations are real. I could read only the abstract. I cannot confirm attack success rates, which models were tested, or whether the defense costs accuracy. The threat also requires a compromised or untrusted teacher. That matters most when teachers are third-party or downloaded checkpoints.

articles.headline: A "leftover" channel helps feature-finding tools stay both faithful and readable
articles.dek: A new paper splits the job of a sparse feature extractor in two: one part keeps the clean concepts, and a second part soaks up everything else.
body: On November 18, 2026, Anh Tien Nguyen, Dimitris Samaras and Mahdi S. Hosseini posted DualSAE to arXiv. <cite index="40-4">It is a modular framework that adds a plug-in Residual Branch to a standard sparse autoencoder.</cite> The authors say this fixes a quiet conflict inside these tools, and they report gains on both vision and language data.

Recall what a sparse autoencoder (SAE) is. It is a small network trained on a larger model's internal activations, the vectors a layer produces. It rewrites each activation as a combination of a few entries from a big dictionary of feature directions. One analogy is a paint-mixing recipe that may use only a handful of colors from a very large palette. A typical recipe has <cite index="45-1">fewer than 100 nonzero numbers</cite>, even though the activation it rebuilds has thousands of dimensions. Interpretability is the hope that each palette color matches one human-readable concept.

The conflict is this. <cite index="40-3">In a traditional SAE, one sparse representation is responsible for both reconstruction fidelity and interpretability, and the two are not guaranteed to align.</cite> Reconstruction fidelity means how closely the rebuilt vector matches the original. A cluttered activation forces the dictionary to carry odd, mixed-up features just to rebuild the details. DualSAE gives those details somewhere else to go. The ordinary SAE stays as the Sparse Branch. <cite index="40-6">The Residual Branch models the non-semantic information the Sparse Branch omits.</cite> The paper also uses <cite index="1-6">a two-stage training strategy that first stabilizes sparse representation learning before coupling it with the Residual Branch.</cite>

The standard objective shows what is being relieved. \[ \mathcal{L} = \lVert x - \hat{x} \rVert_2^2 + \lambda \lVert z \rVert_1 \] This loss rewards accurate rebuilding and penalizes using many features. Here \(x\) is the original activation vector, \(\hat{x}\) is the rebuilt vector with the same shape, \(z\) is the sparse code, with one entry per dictionary feature, and \(\lambda\) is a scalar that sets how hard sparsity is pushed. The \(\ell_1\) norm \(\lVert z \rVert_1\) is the sum of the absolute values of the entries of \(z\). I could not confirm the exact loss DualSAE uses, so the equation above is the standard baseline. In DualSAE the rebuilt vector also draws on the residual branch, so the sparse code no longer has to carry everything.

The results: <cite index="40-7">across diverse encoder-SAE configurations on two vision datasets and two language corpora, DualSAE achieves mean relative improvements of about 29% in reconstruction fidelity and 34% in interpretability, measured by monosemanticity score.</cite> Monosemanticity means a feature responds to one concept. The caveats are real. The interpretability number is an automated proxy, not a human audit. A residual branch could also quietly absorb information that matters, so it is worth checking what ends up there.
articles.why: If interpretability tools must also reconstruct faithfully, they can be forced to choose between accuracy and readability, so architectures that remove that trade-off could make feature-based analysis of large models more trustworthy.

terms.def: A network that rewrites a model's activation vector as a combination of a few dictionary features, in the hope that each feature matches one concept.
How closely the vector rebuilt from the sparse code matches the original activation.
The property that a single feature responds to one concept instead of a mix of unrelated ones.
The sum of the absolute values of a vector's entries, used as a penalty that pushes many entries to zero.
An open online archive where researchers post papers before peer review.

sources.title: Separating Interpretability and Reconstruction in Sparse Autoencoders (arXiv 2611.25165)
An Intuitive Explanation of Sparse Autoencoders for LLM Interpretability

recap: A sparse autoencoder normally has to both rebuild activations and produce readable features, and those goals can pull apart.
DualSAE adds a residual branch to hold non-semantic leftovers, so the sparse branch can stay focused on clean concepts.
The reported gains of roughly 29% and 34% are averages over configurations, and the interpretability measure is a proxy.
deeper: A sparse autoencoder (SAE) is a small network trained on a larger model's activations. An activation is the vector of numbers a layer produces for one input. The SAE rewrites each activation as a mix of a few entries from a big dictionary of feature directions, which are fixed vectors the SAE learns. Picture a paint recipe that may use only a handful of colors from a huge palette. A typical recipe has fewer than 100 nonzero numbers, even though the activation has thousands of dimensions. The hope is interpretability: each palette color matches one concept a person can name. A feature that responds to a single concept is called monosemantic.

On November 18, 2026, Anh Tien Nguyen, Dimitris Samaras and Mahdi S. Hosseini posted DualSAE to arXiv, a public preprint server. DualSAE is a framework that adds a plug-in Residual Branch to a standard SAE. The authors target a quiet conflict. In a traditional SAE, one sparse code must deliver both reconstruction fidelity, meaning how closely the rebuilt vector matches the original, and interpretability. Nothing guarantees those goals agree.

Here is the intuition. Imagine you must copy a photograph using only a few labeled paint tubes. Fine speckles in the photo tempt you to mix a muddy, unlabeled color just to match them. In an SAE, that muddy color is a blended, hard-to-read feature. DualSAE gives the speckles a separate place to go. The ordinary SAE stays on as the Sparse Branch. The Residual Branch models the non-semantic information the Sparse Branch leaves out. The paper also trains in two stages. First the sparse part is stabilized, and only then is it coupled with the residual part. My reading is that this stops the residual from taking over the whole job, though that motive is my inference.
The standard SAE objective shows the burden being relieved.
\[ \mathcal{L} = \lVert x - \hat{x} \rVert_2^2 + \lambda \lVert z \rVert_1 \]

This loss rewards accurate rebuilding and charges a price for every active feature. Here \(x\) is the original activation vector. \(\hat{x}\) is the rebuilt vector, with the same shape as \(x\). \(z\) is the sparse code, with one entry per dictionary feature. \(\lambda\) is a scalar that sets how hard sparsity is pushed. The squared \(\ell_2\) norm \(\lVert \cdot \rVert_2^2\) sums the squared entries of the error. The \(\ell_1\) norm \(\lVert z \rVert_1\) sums the absolute values of the entries of \(z\). I could not confirm DualSAE's exact loss, so this is the baseline. Schematically, the change is:
\[ \hat{x} = \hat{x}_{\text{sparse}} + \hat{x}_{\text{res}} \]

This says the rebuild is the sum of two parts. \(\hat{x}_{\text{sparse}}\) is the Sparse Branch's rebuild from \(z\). \(\hat{x}_{\text{res}}\) is the Residual Branch's contribution. Both have the same shape as \(x\).

A toy example, which I made up and is not from the paper, makes this concrete. Let \(x = (3, 4, 1)\). Suppose the dictionary has two features, \((1,0,0)\) and \((0,1,0)\), and the code is \(z = (3, 4)\). The sparse rebuild is \((3, 4, 0)\). The error is \((0,0,1)\), so the squared error is 1. The \(\ell_1\) norm of \(z\) is \(3 + 4 = 7\). With \(\lambda = 0.1\), the loss is \(1 + 0.1 \times 7 = 1.7\). A lone SAE could cut that error only by adding or distorting a feature to chase the leftover 1. With a residual that supplies \((0,0,1)\), the error drops to 0. The code keeps its two readable entries, and the loss is \(0 + 0.7 = 0.7\).

Earlier approaches faced the same tension within a single code. You could loosen sparsity or widen the dictionary to gain fidelity, but that often costs readability. DualSAE instead adds a second channel for what the dictionary should not have to explain.

The reported results are across several encoder-SAE configurations, on two vision datasets and two language corpora. Mean relative improvements are about 29% in reconstruction fidelity and 34% in interpretability, measured by monosemanticity score.

The caveats are real. The interpretability number is an automated proxy, not a human audit. The residual could also absorb information that matters, such as parts of a real concept, and then the "non-semantic" label would be wrong. It is worth inspecting what ends up in the Residual Branch. A further question is whether the sparse features stay useful for downstream tasks, such as steering a model, when part of the signal lives outside the dictionary.

articles.headline: Rewording the question can beat asking it again, and the theory says how many rewordings you need
articles.dek: A new paper proves that averaging a language model's answers over a handful of equivalent rewritings needs only logarithmically many rewrites.
body: On November 18, 2026, Behrooz Tahmasebi and Melanie Weber posted a 38-page paper on arXiv about test-time symmetrization. <cite index="30-1">It uses forward passes on rewritings of the input and aggregates the resulting answers over the group G of rewritings.</cite> A forward pass is one run of the network from input to output. The weights stay frozen.

Recall that test-time compute means spending extra computation at inference to get better answers. The common recipe is self-consistency, where you sample many reasoning traces from the same prompt and take a majority vote. <cite index="33-3">Existing scaling laws focus on repeated sampling from a fixed prompt, even though many tasks admit multiple equivalent representations of the same problem.</cite> <cite index="33-4">A graph does not depend on how its nodes are numbered, yet language models can change their answers under such rewritings.</cite>

Think of asking five colleagues the same question in five phrasings, instead of asking one colleague five times. The one colleague repeats the same blind spot. Different phrasings expose different ones. The authors make this precise. A group \(G\) is the set of answer-preserving rewrites, such as every relabeling of graph nodes. Averaging over all of them would cost \(|G|\) forward passes, which is usually astronomical. <cite index="32-3">Test-time symmetrization uses only O(log|G|) random rewrites with a few traces each.</cite> \[ n = O(\log |G|) \] This says the number of rewrites needed grows only with the logarithm of the number of possible rewrites. Here \(n\) is the count of random rewrites you run, and \(|G|\) is the number of distinct equivalent rewrites, which is a plain integer. The big-O hides a constant, so this is a scaling statement and not an exact count. Even so, the scale is striking. With \(|G| = 1{,}000{,}000\), \(\log_2 |G|\) is about 20, because \(2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576\). <cite index="32-4">The paper also proves that decoding alone cannot replace rewriting.</cite> <cite index="30-3">The logarithmic scaling is optimal in general.</cite>

On results, <cite index="30-4">at the same number of forward passes, spending them on rewritings is substantially more accurate than repeated sampling whenever the model's answer depends on how the input is written.</cite> <cite index="32-10">Experiments with four model families confirm the scaling law on next-token distributions and its consequences on reasoning traces.</cite> The caveat is built into the method. <cite index="32-11">On SST-2, a sentiment benchmark, the model is at 96% and only 6–8% of queries are sensitive to demonstration order, so symmetrization changes accuracy by less than half a point.</cite> The method helps only where phrasing sensitivity exists. It also assumes you can list rewrites that truly preserve the answer, which can be hard for messy real-world tasks.
articles.why: It gives test-time compute a theoretical footing beyond repeated sampling, and it separates two sources of randomness (decoding and input form) that scaling-law analyses usually blur together.

terms.def: Extra computation spent at inference, such as sampling more answers, to improve a fixed model's output.
Sampling several reasoning traces for the same prompt and taking the most common final answer.
Averaging over transformations that should not change the answer, so the result respects that invariance.
The Stanford Sentiment Treebank 2, a benchmark that asks a model to label movie-review sentences as positive or negative.
An open online archive where researchers post papers before peer review.

sources.title: Test-Time Symmetrization: Scaling Laws for Model-Agnostic Learning under Structure (arXiv 2611.24032)
Test-Time Symmetrization (HTML version)

recap: Instead of sampling the same prompt repeatedly, you can spend your compute on equivalent rewritings of the input and aggregate the answers.
The theory says you need only on the order of the logarithm of the number of possible rewritings, and that this is optimal in general.
The gain appears only when a model's answer actually changes with phrasing, as the near-zero effect on SST-2 shows.
deeper: Start with the prerequisites. A forward pass is one run of a network from input to output. At inference, the weights (the learned numbers inside the network) stay frozen. Test-time compute means spending extra computation at inference to get better answers. The common recipe is self-consistency: sample many reasoning traces (step-by-step texts the model writes before answering) from one prompt, then take a majority vote over the final answers.

Self-consistency has a weakness. Many tasks have several equivalent ways to write the same problem. A graph does not depend on how its nodes are numbered, yet a language model can change its answer when the numbering changes. Sampling repeatedly from one prompt is like asking one colleague the same question five times. They repeat the same blind spot. Asking five colleagues in five phrasings exposes different blind spots.

The paper by Behrooz Tahmasebi and Melanie Weber turns this into a method called test-time symmetrization. A group \(G\) is a set of answer-preserving rewrites, such as every relabeling of a graph's nodes. The mechanism has three steps. First, draw a few rewrites at random from \(G\). Second, run the frozen model on each rewritten input, with a few traces each. Third, aggregate the answers.
The ideal version averages over every rewrite:
\[ \bar f(x) = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} f(g \cdot x) \]

This averages the model's answer distribution across all equivalent versions of the input, so no single phrasing dominates. Here \(x\) is the input. \(g\) is one rewrite from \(G\). \(g \cdot x\) is the input after applying that rewrite. \(f\) is the model's output, a vector of probabilities over the possible answers, with one entry per answer. \(|G|\) is the number of rewrites, a plain integer. \(\bar f(x)\) is the fully averaged answer vector, which has the same shape as \(f\). This is my notation for the idea, not necessarily the paper's.
Computing \(\bar f\) exactly costs \(|G|\) forward passes, which is usually astronomical. The sampled version replaces the sum with \(n\) random rewrites. The paper's central result is:

This says the number of rewrites needed grows only with the logarithm of the number of possible rewrites. Recall that a logarithm counts how many times you double to reach a number. Big-O notation describes how a quantity grows and hides a constant factor. Here \(n\) is the number of random rewrites you run, and \(|G|\) is the number of distinct equivalent rewrites. So this is a scaling statement, not an exact count.

Now a numeric example. Relabel the nodes of a 10-node graph. There are \(10! = 3{,}628{,}800\) orderings, so \(|G| = 3{,}628{,}800\). Since \(2^{21} = 2{,}097{,}152\) and \(2^{22} = 4{,}194{,}304\), \(\log_2 |G|\) is about 22. If the hidden constant were 1, you would need roughly 22 rewrites instead of 3.6 million. With a round \(|G| = 1{,}000{,}000\), \(\log_2 |G|\) is about 20, because \(2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576\). That is a factor of 50,000 fewer passes, since \(1{,}000{,}000 / 20 = 50{,}000\). The real constant will change these counts, so treat them as orders of magnitude.

Compared with earlier approaches, existing scaling laws for test-time compute focus on repeated sampling from a fixed prompt. The paper argues that decoding alone cannot replace rewriting. Decoding is the procedure that turns the model's probabilities into text. Changing how you decode does not remove a bias that comes from how the input was written. The authors also show that logarithmic scaling is optimal in general. At the same number of forward passes, spending them on rewrites is substantially more accurate than repeated sampling whenever the answer depends on how the input is written. Experiments with four model families confirm the scaling law on next-token distributions and its consequences on reasoning traces.

The limits matter. The method helps only where phrasing sensitivity exists. On SST-2, a sentiment benchmark, the model is already at 96%, and only 6–8% of queries are sensitive to demonstration order, meaning the order of the worked examples placed in the prompt. Symmetrization therefore changes accuracy by less than half a point.

The open question is the group itself. The method assumes you can list rewrites that truly preserve the answer. For graph relabeling that is easy. For messy real-world tasks, a paraphrase can quietly change the meaning, and then the average mixes answers to different questions.

articles.headline: A laptop-sized open model reuses its middle layers three times to think harder without writing more
articles.dek: Thinking Machines Lab's Inkling 2 Mini stores 24 layers but runs 12 of them three times per token. That lets a 26-billion-parameter model match a much more compute-hungry rival on one independent benchmark index.
body: <cite index="32-1">Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20, 2026. It is an open-weights model built on a looped transformer, published under Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face.</cite> Open weights means anyone can download the trained parameters and run them. <cite index="31-6">It takes text and image input and has a 1M-token context window.</cite> <cite index="14-11,14-13">The whole model takes up about 20 gigabytes and runs through Ollama on Macs with at least 32 gigabytes of memory.</cite>

Recall that a transformer passes each token through a stack of layers, each with its own weights. A mixture of experts (MoE) is a layer that sends each token to a few of many smaller networks. So only some of the stored parameters are active for any one token. A looped transformer adds a second trick: it reuses the same layers more than once. Think of rereading a hard paragraph with the same brain, instead of hiring a second reader.

<cite index="31-10">Twelve of the model's 24 layers run three times per token. This adds compute without adding output tokens.</cite> The other 12 run once. That makes 12 + 12 × 3 = 48 layer passes from 24 stored layers. In symbols, the looped block applies one function repeatedly: \[ h_{r+1} = F(h_r), \quad r = 0, 1, 2 \] This says the hidden state after each pass is the same 12-layer stack applied to the previous state. Here \(h_r\) is the hidden-state vector for one token (length equal to the model width) entering pass \(r\). \(F\) is the shared middle stack, and \(r\) counts passes. <cite index="32-2">Each extra pass adds about 1.0B effective active parameters. Three passes give 5.4B per token.</cite> That fits the arithmetic: 3.4B + 1.0B + 1.0B = 5.4B. Memory stays tied to the stored weights, so the looping costs time rather than space.

<cite index="32-3">Thinking Machines says it leads open-weights models under 100B total parameters, with 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 46.5% on Vals Index v2.2.</cite> Both are agentic-coding evaluations. <cite index="31-7,31-9">Artificial Analysis, an independent benchmarking firm, says the model matches Qwen3.8 27B on its Intelligence Index with about five times fewer active parameters. It uses about 38% more output tokens but roughly 2.8 times less compute.</cite> <cite index="32-4">The lab also reports that looping the middle 12 layers beat looping the last layers on 27 of 28 evaluations.</cite> The caveats matter. <cite index="32-5">It trails Qwen3.8-27B on MultiChallenge and ComplexConstraints, and it trails larger models on CritPt v2 and HLE-Diamond.</cite> Most numbers come from the lab itself, and independent testing has only just begun.
articles.why: It is an open, permissively licensed test of whether repeating layers is a better way to buy reasoning than adding parameters or output tokens on local hardware.

terms.def: A layer that sends each token to a few of many smaller networks, so only part of the model is active per token.
A transformer that runs some of its layers several times on each token, reusing the same weights.
The weights actually used to process one token, as opposed to all weights stored.
Trained parameters released for download, so anyone can run and fine-tune the model.
A composite score from an independent firm that combines many model evaluations.

sources.title: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, an open looped transformer that runs on a laptop
Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini, an open weights looped transformer

recap: Inkling 2 Mini stores 24 layers but runs its middle 12 three times per token, so it does 48 layer passes.
Looping spends extra compute instead of extra memory or extra written reasoning, which suits a 20-gigabyte laptop model.
The strongest claims come from the lab and one early independent index, and the model trails on multi-constraint instruction following.
deeper: Start with the basics. A token is a small chunk of text or image that the model reads. A transformer is a stack of layers, and each layer updates a vector for every token. That vector is called the hidden state, and its length is the model width. Parameters are the learned numbers inside the layers. A mixture of experts (MoE) is a layer that sends each token to a few of many smaller networks, so only some stored parameters are active for any one token. Open weights means anyone can download the trained parameters and run them.

Thinking Machines Lab released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20, 2026. It is an open-weights model, published under the Apache 2.0 license (a permissive software license) on Hugging Face (a site for sharing models). It accepts text and image input and has a 1M-token context window, meaning it can read about a million tokens at once. The model takes up about 20 gigabytes. It runs through Ollama, a tool for running models locally, on Macs with at least 32 gigabytes of memory.

Now the mechanism. Many models "think harder" by writing out more reasoning tokens, which is slow and costly to read. A looped transformer does something different. Picture rereading a hard paragraph with the same brain, instead of hiring a second reader. The model sends a token's hidden state through the same layers more than once. Here, 12 of the 24 layers run three times per token, and the other 12 run once. So the model stores 24 layers but performs 12 + 12 × 3 = 48 layer passes. The extra thinking happens inside the network, so it adds compute without adding output tokens.
The math is short. The looped block applies one function repeatedly:

This says each pass takes the current hidden state and refines it with the same stack of layers. Here \(h_r\) is the hidden-state vector for one token entering pass \(r\), with length equal to the model width. \(F\) is the shared 12-layer middle stack. Because every pass uses the same \(F\), the weights are stored once. The index \(r\) counts passes, so three passes produce \(h_1\), \(h_2\), and \(h_3\).
Compute counts the same way. Each extra pass adds about 1.0B effective active parameters, where B means billions:
\[ P_{\text{active}} = 3.4\text{B} + 2 \times 1.0\text{B} = 5.4\text{B} \]

This says the work done per token is the first pass plus two repeats. \(P_{\text{active}}\) is the effective number of active parameters per token, in billions. The 3.4B is the cost of a single pass through the whole model. Each 1.0B is the cost of one repeat of the shared block. Memory tracks the stored weights, so looping costs time rather than space.

A rough check shows the trade. Artificial Analysis, an independent benchmarking firm, says the model matches Qwen3.8 27B (a 27B-parameter open model) on its Intelligence Index. Since 27 / 5.4 = 5, that is five times fewer active parameters. The model also writes about 38% more output tokens, or 1.38 times as many. A parameter-only estimate gives 1.38 × 0.2 = 0.276 of the compute, about 3.6 times less. The reported figure is roughly 2.8 times less, so parameters alone do not capture the full cost.

Compared with a dense model, which uses all its parameters for every token, this design is far lighter per pass. Compared with an MoE alone, it adds depth without adding stored weights. Compared with reasoning models that write long chains of thought, it moves some thinking out of the visible text. The lab also reports that looping the middle 12 layers beat looping the last layers on 27 of 28 evaluations. That suggests the middle of the stack is a good place to repeat work.

Thinking Machines says the model leads open-weights models under 100B total parameters, with 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 46.5% on Vals Index v2.2. Both are agentic-coding evaluations, which test whether a model can complete multi-step programming tasks. The caveats matter. It trails Qwen3.8-27B on MultiChallenge and ComplexConstraints. It also trails larger models on CritPt v2 and HLE-Diamond. Most numbers come from the lab itself, and independent testing has only just begun.

Open questions remain. Is three passes the best choice, or would the model gain more from a variable number per token? How much do repeated passes help tasks that need new knowledge rather than more reasoning? And does the extra latency matter on a laptop, where each pass takes real time?

articles.headline: Where the small model places its guesses matters: same budget, 2.02× instead of 1.46× faster generation
articles.dek: A new paper shows that a fixed budget of speculative guesses runs much faster when the guesses go to branches the small model is confident about.
body: On November 17, 2026, Hadi Fares, Mayssa Hajj Hassan, Ali Salman and Ammar Mohanna posted FACT (Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training) on arXiv. <cite index="41-3">It is an experimental framework for studying how drafter training, candidate allocation and execution conditions affect acceptance and latency.</cite> <cite index="41-4">They use a lightweight feature-prediction drafter with a frozen Llama-3-8B-Instruct target under greedy decoding.</cite> Greedy decoding means always picking the single most likely next token.

Recall that a language model normally writes one token per forward pass, which is slow. Speculative decoding speeds this up. <cite index="41-1">A cheap drafter proposes tokens, and the large target model verifies multiple draft tokens in a single pass.</cite> Think of a sous-chef laying out likely next steps while the head chef approves them in one glance. In the tree version, the drafter proposes branching alternatives. The target checks them all at once, up to a fixed number of tree nodes.

The question is where to spend that node budget. A static allocation gives every depth a fixed quota of branches, however sure the drafter is. Confidence-guided allocation ranks candidates instead. <cite index="42-5">It scores a continuation by cumulative draft confidence.</cite> One natural way to write that is \[ s(y_{1:d}) = \prod_{i=1}^{d} q_i \] This multiplies the drafter's probabilities along a path, so a path is only as believable as its weakest steps. Here \(y_{1:d}\) is the candidate path of \(d\) tokens, and \(q_i\) is the drafter's probability for the \(i\)-th token given the earlier ones, a number between 0 and 1. For example, probabilities 0.9, 0.8 and 0.7 give 0.9 × 0.8 × 0.7 = 0.504. The paper's example is a prompt that continues with "Paris". <cite index="42-10">Static quotas miss the target's comma continuation and accept two tokens. Confidence-guided selection puts both depth-3 slots below "Paris" and accepts three.</cite>

<cite index="41-5">With a fixed 256-node budget and matched per-depth widths, confidence-guided allocation raises speedup over autoregressive decoding from 1.46× to 2.02× on HumanEval, a code benchmark. On MT-Bench, a multi-turn chat benchmark, it raises it from 1.31× to 1.75×.</cite> <cite index="42-4">It reduces latency without increasing candidate counts at any depth.</cite> The limits are clear. <cite index="42-1">The method transfers to an independently trained drafter, but its benefit does not consistently grow with drafter strength.</cite> <cite index="42-3">Rollout training improves acceptance, but proxy loss can misrank drafters.</cite> The abstract reports a single 8-billion-parameter target and greedy decoding. Whether the gains hold for sampling, larger targets or busy production batches is not shown there.
articles.why: Serving systems that use speculative decoding can gain speed just by reallocating a fixed verification budget, and the paper argues for judging drafters on end-to-end latency rather than acceptance alone.

terms.def: A speed-up where a small model drafts several tokens and the large model verifies them in one pass.
The small, cheap model that proposes candidate tokens for the large target model to check.
Generating text by always choosing the single most probable next token.
A branching set of candidate continuations that the target model verifies together in one forward pass.
The share of drafted tokens that the target model confirms and keeps.

sources.title: FACT: Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training for Speculative Decoding (arXiv abstract)
FACT: Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training for Speculative Decoding (full text)

recap: Speculative decoding speeds up generation by letting a small drafter guess tokens that a large model checks in one pass.
With the node budget held at 256, spending it on high-confidence branches raised speedup from 1.46× to 2.02× on HumanEval.
The result comes from one 8-billion-parameter target under greedy decoding, so wider claims are unproven.
deeper: Recall that a language model normally writes one token, a small chunk of text such as a word piece, per forward pass, meaning one full run of the network. That is slow because each pass must wait for the last. Speculative decoding breaks the wait. A cheap drafter model guesses several upcoming tokens, and the large target model checks them all in a single pass. The output stays what the target would have produced, because the target has the final say.

On November 17, 2026, Hadi Fares, Mayssa Hajj Hassan, Ali Salman and Ammar Mohanna posted FACT (Fixed-Budget Allocation and Cross-Step Training) on arXiv, a public preprint server. FACT is an experimental framework for studying how drafter training, candidate allocation and execution conditions affect two things. Acceptance is how many drafted tokens the target keeps. Latency is the wait per generated token. The drafter is lightweight and predicts features, meaning the target's internal vectors, rather than only words. The target is Llama-3-8B-Instruct, an 8-billion-parameter chat model, kept frozen, so its weights never change. Decoding is greedy, meaning the model always picks the single most likely next token.

Think of a sous-chef laying out likely next steps while the head chef approves them in one glance. In the tree version, the sous-chef lays out branching alternatives. The target checks every branch at once, up to a fixed number of tree nodes, where each node is one candidate token at one position. The real question is where to spend that node budget.

A static allocation gives every depth, meaning position in the draft, a fixed quota of branches. It does this however sure the drafter is. That wastes slots. If the drafter is nearly certain about the first token, a wide fan-out there buys little. A deeper position, where the drafter is torn between two continuations, may get too few slots.
Confidence-guided allocation ranks candidate paths and keeps the best ones until the budget runs out. The paper scores a continuation by cumulative draft confidence. One natural way to write that is

This multiplies the drafter's probabilities along a path, so a path is only as believable as its weakest steps. Here \(s\) is the path's score, a single number between 0 and 1. The symbol \(y_{1:d}\) is the candidate path of \(d\) tokens. The index \(i\) counts positions from 1 to \(d\). The symbol \(q_i\) is the drafter's probability for the \(i\)-th token given the earlier ones, also between 0 and 1.

Take two paths of three tokens. Probabilities 0.9, 0.8 and 0.7 give 0.9 × 0.8 × 0.7 = 0.504. Probabilities 0.6, 0.5 and 0.4 give 0.6 × 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.12. The first path earns a slot well before the second, even if the second sits at a depth where a static rule would have reserved one for it. These numbers are illustrative, not from the paper.

The paper's own example is a prompt that continues with "Paris". Static quotas miss the target's comma continuation and accept two tokens. Confidence-guided selection puts both depth-3 slots below "Paris" and accepts three. At scale, with a fixed 256-node budget and matched per-depth widths, speedup over autoregressive decoding, the plain one-token-at-a-time baseline, rises from 1.46× to 2.02× on HumanEval, a code benchmark. On MT-Bench, a multi-turn chat benchmark, it rises from 1.31× to 1.75×. Candidate counts at each depth do not increase. The gain comes only from placement.
Compared with static trees, the change is small in mechanism. Both spend the same budget. The difference is that confidence decides where the nodes go, not a fixed schedule.

The limits are clear. The method transfers to an independently trained drafter, but its benefit does not consistently grow with drafter strength. Rollout training, which trains the drafter on its own multi-step guesses, improves acceptance. But proxy loss, the cheap training-time stand-in for real speed, can misrank drafters. So a lower loss does not guarantee a faster system.

Scope matters too. The abstract reports a single 8-billion-parameter target and greedy decoding. Whether the gains hold for sampling, where the next token is drawn at random, or for larger targets is not shown there. Nor is it shown for busy production batches, where many requests share one pass and spare compute is scarce.

articles.headline: A 552-Billion-Parameter Brain, Frozen, Now Steers a Robot Arm
articles.dek: A new preprint bolts a small trainable motion generator onto a huge frozen language-and-vision model, and tests whether bigger backbones help robots.
body: On November 16, 2026, a team led by Ruixi Yu posted ScaleVLA. <cite index="47-4">It scales the vision-language backbone of a learned robot policy to 552 billion parameters, using DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017.</cite> A vision-language-action (VLA) model reads camera images and an instruction and outputs robot actions. A vision-language model (VLM) reads images and text and answers in text. <cite index="47-10">The backbone here is a mixture-of-experts (MoE) model, a network that routes each token to a few of many smaller sub-networks.</cite>

Recall the usual recipe. Take a VLM that has absorbed web-scale knowledge, then attach an action head that turns its internal features into motion. Most VLA policies use small backbones. The authors argue that this <cite index="50-6">leaves the potential of frontier models largely untapped.</cite> The action head is a diffusion transformer (DiT), a transformer that generates outputs by gradually denoising. It is trained with flow matching, which teaches a network a velocity that carries random noise toward a real action chunk, meaning a short run of future actions emitted together.

Picture a senior consultant who reads the scene once and writes briefing notes. A fast junior then turns the notes into motions. <cite index="47-7">ScaleVLA does not reason in text: it reads the backbone once per action chunk and maps its representations directly to actions.</cite> <cite index="47-8">The language and visual backbones are frozen, while the feature adapter, state and action encoders, diffusion transformer, and action decoder are trainable.</cite> The standard flow-matching loss is\[ \mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}\,\big\|v_\theta(x_t,t,c)-(a-\epsilon)\big\|^2,\quad x_t=(1-t)\epsilon+t\,a. \]This loss trains the head to point from noise toward the true action. Here \(a\) is the true action chunk (a vector), \(\epsilon\) is random noise of the same shape, \(t\in[0,1]\) is the blend time, \(x_t\) is the noisy mix, \(c\) is the backbone features plus robot state, and \(v_\theta\) is the head's predicted velocity. For example, if \(a=1.0\), \(\epsilon=0.2\) and \(t=0.5\), then \(x_t=0.6\) and the target velocity is 0.8. This is the generic form of the objective. I did not confirm the paper's exact convention.

<cite index="47-5">The team compared backbones from 2B to 552B parameters, holding the action architecture, initialization, demonstrations and optimization budget fixed.</cite> <cite index="47-3">Despite its scale, ScaleVLA reaches a median latency of 216 milliseconds per action chunk.</cite> <cite index="49-10">It achieves the highest overall LIBERO-PRO mean success under perturbations, at 45.1%.</cite> LIBERO-PRO is a manipulation benchmark that perturbs the scene. <cite index="49-9">Object perturbations stay hard for every model, with the best entry at 32.4%.</cite> Caveats: this is a preprint. Absolute success under perturbation is still below 50%. A frozen backbone also leaves open whether fine-tuning it would help further.
articles.why: It tests directly whether frontier-scale language knowledge transfers to robot control when everything else in the policy is held fixed.

sources.title: ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters (arXiv HTML)
ScaleVLA (arXiv abstract page, submitted 16 Nov 2026)

recap: ScaleVLA pairs a frozen 552-billion-parameter vision-language model with a small trainable flow-matching action head.
It reads the huge backbone once per action chunk, which keeps median latency at 216 milliseconds.
Scale helps, but robustness to perturbed scenes remains weak, with 45.1% mean success on LIBERO-PRO.
deeper: On November 16, 2026, a team led by Ruixi Yu posted ScaleVLA, a robot policy whose language-and-vision backbone has 552 billion parameters. The backbone comes from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, a large language model built as a mixture of experts.

First, the prerequisites. A vision-language model (VLM) reads images and text and answers in text. A vision-language-action (VLA) model reads camera images plus an instruction and outputs robot actions. A mixture of experts (MoE) is a layer that sends each token, a small chunk of input, to a few of many smaller sub-networks. The usual VLA recipe takes a VLM that has absorbed web-scale knowledge and attaches an action head, a module that turns internal features into motion. Most VLA policies use small backbones. The authors argue this leaves the potential of frontier models largely untapped.

Now the mechanism. Picture a senior consultant who reads the scene once and writes briefing notes. A fast junior then turns the notes into motions. The backbone is the consultant. It does not reason in text. It reads the images and instruction once per action chunk, meaning a short run of future actions emitted together. It maps its internal representations directly to actions.

The junior is a diffusion transformer (DiT). A transformer is a network built from attention layers, and a diffusion model generates outputs by gradually denoising. The language and visual backbones are frozen, meaning their weights are not updated. The feature adapter, state and action encoders, diffusion transformer, and action decoder are trainable.

Training uses flow matching. Imagine a straight path from a random noise vector to a real action chunk. The network learns the velocity, the direction and speed of travel along that path, at any point. The generic loss is:
\[ \mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}\,\big\|v_\theta(x_t,t,c)-(a-\epsilon)\big\|^2,\quad x_t=(1-t)\epsilon+t\,a. \]

This trains the head to point from noise toward the true action. Here \(a\) is the true action chunk, a vector. \(\epsilon\) is random noise with the same shape as \(a\). The number \(t\in[0,1]\) is the blend time, where 0 is pure noise and 1 is the real action. \(x_t\) is the noisy mix, with the same shape as \(a\). The context \(c\) is the backbone features plus the robot state. \(v_\theta\) is the head's predicted velocity, with the same shape as \(a\), and \(\theta\) stands for its trainable weights. \(\mathbb{E}\) is an average over training examples, noise draws, and times. The double bars with the square measure squared distance between prediction and target. The target is \(a-\epsilon\) because it is the rate of change of \(x_t\) as \(t\) grows. I did not confirm the paper's exact convention.

A numeric example makes this concrete. Take \(a=1.0\), \(\epsilon=0.2\), and \(t=0.5\). Then \(x_t=0.5\times0.2+0.5\times1.0=0.6\), and the target velocity is \(1.0-0.2=0.8\). If the head predicted 0.5, the error would be 0.3, and the squared error would be 0.09. At run time the head starts from noise and takes small steps along its predicted velocity. With a perfect constant velocity of 0.8 over a total time of 1, the value moves from 0.2 to 1.0, which is the true action.

Compared with earlier work, the change is the size of the backbone, not the action design. The team compared backbones from 2B to 552B parameters. They held the action architecture, initialization, demonstrations, and optimization budget fixed. That isolates backbone size as the variable. Despite its scale, ScaleVLA reaches a median latency, the middle time to produce one result, of 216 milliseconds per action chunk. Two things plausibly help, though the brief does not say so. Each MoE token activates only a few experts, and one backbone read serves a whole chunk.

On LIBERO-PRO, a manipulation benchmark that perturbs the scene, ScaleVLA achieves the highest overall mean success under perturbations, at 45.1%. Object perturbations stay hard for every model, with the best entry at 32.4%.

The limits are clear. This is a preprint, so it has not been peer reviewed. Absolute success under perturbation is still below 50%. A frozen backbone also leaves open whether fine-tuning it, meaning continuing to train its weights on robot data, would help further.

articles.headline: Robot Action Generators Can Use Fewer Bits Early and More Bits Late
articles.dek: A chip-design paper shows that the early denoising steps of a robot's motion generator tolerate coarser numbers than the final steps.
body: On November 18, 2026, Robin Geens, Marian Verhelst and colleagues posted a paper on speeding up robot policies in hardware. It targets the action head of a vision-language-action (VLA) model, a network that reads images and an instruction and outputs robot motion. <cite index="40-3">In models such as GR00T, the action head is a diffusion transformer that turns noise into a chunk of actions in a few flow-matching steps.</cite>

Recall that quantization stores weights with fewer bits, for example 4 instead of 16, which shrinks memory traffic. Here is why that matters. <cite index="40-4,40-5">Every step re-reads all of the head's weights from dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), the main off-chip memory, but applies each weight to only about fifty tokens. Inference is therefore memory-bound, so latency and energy track the total weight bits transferred.</cite> It is like a courier who drives to the warehouse for every small parcel. The trip, not the parcel, costs the time.

The key observation is that the steps need not share one precision. Think of sculpting: early rough cuts can be sloppy, because later cuts fix them. <cite index="39-9">An action head's output barely depends on its starting noise, so early steps tolerate more quantization than late ones.</cite> <cite index="38-1">Later flow steps attenuate the quantization errors of earlier steps, so precision should rise over the steps.</cite> The cost is measured in bit-steps, the bits read per weight summed over all steps:\[ B=W\sum_{k=1}^{N} b_k. \]This number is proportional to the memory traffic, and so to the latency and energy. \(W\) is the number of weights, \(N\) is the number of flow steps, and \(b_k\) is the bits per weight at step \(k\). For four steps at widths 2, 3, 3 and 4 bits, the sum is 12 bits per weight. Uniform 4-bit weights would need 16, so <cite index="40-6">the rising widths transfer 25% fewer bits than 4-bit weights at every step.</cite> The authors also built an accelerator. <cite index="40-8,40-9">It decodes entropy-coded weights for bit-serial sub-arrays at the DRAM rate. A run-time allocator divides those sub-arrays between the linear layers and attention as widths change.</cite> Bit-serial means the hardware processes one bit of each weight per cycle.

<cite index="39-4">With plain per-channel rounding, and no calibration or training, widths rising from 2 to 4 bits preserve the closed-loop success of robot policies.</cite> Closed-loop means the policy actually controls the robot, in simulation, and its errors feed back into later observations. <cite index="7-1">In simulation with realistic memory timing, the design runs the GR00T N1.6 action head in 8.02 milliseconds per inference, using 2, 3, 3 and 4 bits across its four steps.</cite> Caveats: these are simulated hardware numbers, not fabricated silicon. The success results come from the paper's screening benchmarks, and I could not confirm which ones. Whether the pattern holds for other action heads is still unproven.
articles.why: Real-time robot control is bound by memory bandwidth on the robot, and this gives a training-free way to cut it.
