sources.title: Hardware Acceleration of Vision-Language-Action Models with Weight Precision Rising over the Flow Steps (arXiv abstract)
Hardware Acceleration of Vision-Language-Action Models with Weight Precision Rising over the Flow Steps (arXiv HTML)

recap: A robot's action head re-reads all its weights at every denoising step, so it is limited by memory traffic, not arithmetic.
Early steps tolerate coarser weights because later steps correct their errors, so bit widths of 2, 3, 3 and 4 work across four steps.
That schedule moves 25% fewer bits than uniform 4-bit weights, but the results are simulated and not yet shown on real chips.
deeper: Start with the setting. A vision-language-action (VLA) model is a network that reads camera images and a text instruction and outputs robot motion. Its final part, the action head, produces a chunk of future actions at once. In models such as GR00T (a robot foundation model whose action head is a diffusion transformer), the head starts from random noise and refines it into actions. Recall that a transformer is a stack of layers where tokens, the small vectors that represent pieces of input, attend to one another. Flow matching trains the network to push noise toward data along a smooth path. At inference you take a few small steps along that path, and the head runs once per step.

Now the bottleneck. Every step re-reads all of the head's weights from dynamic random-access memory (DRAM), the large off-chip memory. Yet each weight is used on only about fifty tokens. Compare a courier who drives to the warehouse for every small parcel. The trip costs the time, not the parcel. Engineers call this memory-bound: latency (time per inference) and energy track the number of weight bits moved, not the arithmetic. Quantization, which stores each weight with fewer bits such as 4 instead of 16, cuts that traffic.

The new idea, from a paper posted on November 18, 2026 by Robin Geens, Marian Verhelst and colleagues, is that the steps need not share one precision. Picture sculpting. Early rough cuts can be sloppy because later cuts fix them. Two facts support this. The head's output barely depends on its starting noise, so early steps tolerate coarse weights. And later flow steps attenuate, meaning shrink, the errors left by earlier steps. So precision should rise over the steps.
To compare schedules, the authors count bit-steps, the bits read per weight summed over all steps:

This says total memory traffic is the number of weights times the bits each one costs at each step, added up. Here \(B\) is total bits transferred (a count of bits), \(W\) is the number of weights (a scalar), \(N\) is the number of flow steps (a scalar), \(k\) is the step index from 1 to \(N\), and \(b_k\) is the bits per weight at step \(k\). Because \(B\) is proportional to traffic, it is also proportional to latency and energy.

A small example makes it concrete. Use four steps with widths 2, 3, 3 and 4 bits. The sum is \(2+3+3+4=12\) bits per weight. Uniform 4-bit weights would need \(4\times4=16\). The saving is \((16-12)/16=0.25\), or 25% fewer bits, for any \(W\), since \(W\) cancels in the ratio.

The authors also built an accelerator to realize the saving. It decodes entropy-coded weights, meaning weights compressed so common values take fewer bits, at the DRAM rate. These feed bit-serial sub-arrays, compute units that process one bit of each weight per cycle. Bit-serial hardware suits mixed widths, because a 2-bit weight simply takes fewer cycles than a 4-bit one. A run-time allocator divides the sub-arrays between the linear layers and attention as the widths change.

Compared with earlier approaches, the quantizer is plain. It uses per-channel rounding, where each output channel of a weight matrix gets its own scale and values are rounded to the nearest level. It needs no calibration (tuning on sample data) and no retraining. A common baseline gives every step the same width. This schedule varies width over time instead. The authors report that widths rising from 2 to 4 bits preserve closed-loop success. Closed-loop means the policy actually controls the robot in simulation, so its errors feed into later observations. In simulation with realistic memory timing, the design runs the GR00T N1.6 action head in 8.02 milliseconds per inference, using 2, 3, 3 and 4 bits across its four steps.

Several limits apply. These are simulated hardware numbers, not fabricated silicon. The success results come from the paper's screening benchmarks, and I could not confirm which ones. Whether the pattern holds for other action heads remains unproven. It is also unclear how much the schedule depends on using four steps.

articles.headline: A neural network reads a child's brain-tumor chemistry to forecast survival year by year
articles.dek: A Nature Genetics paper from Dana-Farber describes a model that turns routine tumor tests into a personal 10-year survival curve and suggests which children might safely get less radiation.
body: Sabina Stefan, Volker Hovestadt and colleagues at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute reported MANTIS in Nature Genetics on 3 November 2026. <cite index="43-1">MANTIS is a precision artificial intelligence (AI) tool, built on genome-wide DNA methylation array data from 2,786 patients.</cite> The idea is to reuse measurements that hospitals already take. Think of a methylation array as a very long fingerprint of the tumor. The network learns which parts of the fingerprint go with long or short survival. <cite index="40-4,40-5">The released code uses a sparse input layer guided by a gene-connectivity prior, plus a multi-task logistic regression (MTLR) head for discrete-time survival.</cite> The sparse layer connects each input only to a few related units, which suits tens of thousands of inputs and few patients.

The MTLR head splits the 10 years into \(K\) intervals. With hidden representation \(z\), set \(s_j = \theta_j^\top z + b_j\). Then \[P(\text{event in interval } k \mid x) = \frac{\exp\big(\sum_{j=k}^{K} s_j\big)}{\sum_{m=1}^{K+1} \exp\big(\sum_{j=m}^{K} s_j\big)}.\] This turns one score per interval into a probability for each possible event time. The case \(m=K+1\) means the patient survives past the horizon, so its sum is empty and its numerator is 1. Here \(z\) is a learned vector summarizing the tumor, \(\theta_j\) is a weight vector of the same length, \(b_j\) is a scalar bias, and \(K\) is the number of time bins. For example, take \(K=2\), \(s_1=0\) and \(s_2=\ln 2\). The three numerators are 2, 2 and 1, which sum to 5. The probabilities are 0.4, 0.4 and 0.2, so predicted survival past the horizon is 0.2.

On validation, <cite index="39-3">MANTIS reached concordance indices up to 0.80 ± 0.07, above the accuracy of current clinical indicators.</cite> The concordance index is the chance that, for a random pair of patients, the model ranks the one who died sooner as higher risk. A value of 0.5 is a coin flip. To go from prognosis to treatment, the authors <cite index="43-6">fed variational autoencoder (VAE) representations into a small network with the same survival output.</cite> A VAE is a network that compresses each input into a short code and reconstructs it. They then estimated how survival would change under different radiation doses. <cite index="39-5">About 60% of average-risk medulloblastoma patients showed no significant survival disadvantage (P = .683) with lower-dose craniospinal irradiation, radiation to the brain and spine.</cite> A non-significant difference is not proof of equivalence, so this is a hypothesis for trials.
articles.why: It shows deep learning adding value on top of a test hospitals already run, with a concrete aim of sparing children some treatment harm.

terms.def: Software that learns patterns from data to make predictions or decisions.
An output layer that predicts a whole survival curve by assigning probabilities to event times in discrete time bins.
A network that compresses each input into a short probabilistic code and learns to reconstruct the input from it.
The fraction of patient pairs where the model correctly ranks who has the shorter survival; 0.5 is chance, 1.0 is perfect.
The molecule that carries genetic instructions in cells.

sources.title: AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization for childhood brain tumors (Nature Genetics)
Pediatric Brain Tumors: Prognostic AI Model Guides Precision Therapy Choices (The ASCO Post)
sstefan01/methylation-survival: MANTIS v1.0.0 (Zenodo)

background: Medulloblastoma and ependymoma are malignant brain tumors in children. <cite index="34-7">Medulloblastoma is one of the most common of these tumors, and ependymoma is another whose outcomes vary widely.</cite> Treatment is a trade-off. <cite index="33-6">Therapy must be strong enough to stop the cancer returning, but it can also cause lasting harm to learning, development and quality of life.</cite> Doctors therefore try to sort children into risk groups, so that low-risk children get gentler treatment. Those groups are coarse, and children in the same group can have very different outcomes.

The mathematics of the task is survival analysis. For a patient with features \(x\), we want the survival function \(S(t \mid x) = P(T > t \mid x)\). Here \(T\) is the time until death. Some patients are still alive when follow-up ends, and this is called censoring: we only know \(T\) is larger than the last check-up. Kaplan and Meier (1958) gave a nonparametric way to estimate survival curves for whole groups. Cox (1972) introduced proportional hazards regression for patient features. Yu and colleagues (2011) proposed multi-task logistic regression, which predicts a full curve instead of a single risk number. On the biology side, Capper and colleagues (2018, Nature) showed that deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) methylation, chemical tags on DNA that mark which genes are switched off, can classify brain tumors in routine care. That work classified tumors. It did not forecast survival.
articles.status: The work is peer-reviewed and published in Nature Genetics on 3 November 2026, and the code is released on Zenodo, but the sources I found show retrospective validation and radiation-dose modeling on existing data rather than a prospective clinical trial.
recap: MANTIS is a neural network that turns routine tumor methylation data into an individual survival curve for children with two brain-tumor types.
It was trained on 2,786 patients and reached concordance indices of up to 0.80 in validation cohorts.
Its suggestion that about 60% of average-risk medulloblastoma patients could get lower-dose radiation is a hypothesis that still needs prospective testing.
deeper: Start with the prerequisites. Survival analysis asks how long until an event, here death. The survival function \(S(t \mid x) = P(T > t \mid x)\) is the probability that the time of death \(T\) exceeds \(t\), given patient features \(x\). Some children are still alive when follow-up ends. This is censoring: we only know \(T\) is larger than the last check-up. The Kaplan-Meier method estimates one survival curve for a whole group without assuming a curve shape. Cox proportional hazards regression instead uses patient features to scale a risk rate, but it outputs one risk number per patient. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) methylation means chemical tags on DNA that mark which genes are switched off. A methylation array measures these tags at tens of thousands of sites. Think of it as a long fingerprint of the tumor.

MANTIS, a neural network from Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, learns which parts of that fingerprint go with long or short survival. It was trained on arrays from 2,786 children with brain tumors. The first difficulty is that there are far more inputs than patients. A sparse layer helps here. It connects each input to only a few related hidden units, chosen using a prior built from how genes connect to one another. A prior is knowledge fixed before training. Fewer connections means fewer weights to fit, so the network overfits less. The sparse layer produces a hidden representation \(z\), a learned vector that summarizes the tumor.

The second step turns \(z\) into a whole survival curve. The multi-task logistic regression (MTLR) head, a final layer that predicts a probability for every possible event time, splits 10 years into \(K\) intervals. It computes one score per interval:
\[ s_j = \theta_j^\top z + b_j. \]

This is a linear read-out of the tumor summary for interval \(j\). Here \(z\) is the hidden vector, \(\theta_j\) is a learned weight vector of the same length as \(z\), and \(b_j\) is a learned scalar bias. The probability of an event in interval \(k\) is then
\[ P(\text{event in interval } k \mid x) = \frac{\exp\big(\sum_{j=k}^{K} s_j\big)}{\sum_{m=1}^{K+1} \exp\big(\sum_{j=m}^{K} s_j\big)}. \]

This is a softmax, which exponentiates scores and divides by their total so the results sum to 1. Each possible event time gets a probability. The index \(k\) is the interval in question, \(m\) runs over all \(K+1\) outcomes, and \(\exp\) is the exponential function. The outcome \(m=K+1\) means the child survives past the horizon. Its sum is empty, so its term is \(\exp(0)=1\). Survival at the end of interval \(k\) is the total probability of all later outcomes.

A small example makes this concrete. Take \(K=2\), \(s_1=0\) and \(s_2=\ln 2\). The three terms are \(\exp(s_1+s_2)=2\), \(\exp(s_2)=2\) and \(1\). They sum to 5, so the probabilities are 0.4, 0.4 and 0.2. Survival past the horizon is 0.2. Survival past the end of interval 1 is \(0.4+0.2=0.6\).

For treatment questions, the authors fed variational autoencoder (VAE) representations into a small network with the same survival output. Recall that a VAE compresses each input into a short code and reconstructs it. They then estimated how survival would change under different radiation doses. About 60% of average-risk medulloblastoma patients showed no significant survival disadvantage (p-value 0.683) with lower-dose craniospinal irradiation, which is radiation to the brain and spine. A p-value is the probability of a difference at least this large if there were truly none.

Compared with earlier work, the change is in what is predicted and from what. Kaplan-Meier gives group curves. Cox gives one risk number per patient. MTLR gives a full curve for each patient. Capper and colleagues showed that methylation can classify tumors, and MANTIS uses the same routine measurements to forecast outcome. Its reported concordance index reached up to 0.80 ± 0.07, above current clinical indicators. The concordance index is the chance that, for a random comparable pair, the model ranks the child who died sooner as higher risk. A value of 0.5 is a coin flip.

The limits matter. A concordance index judges ranking, not whether the predicted probabilities are calibrated. The dose result is an estimate about what might have happened, built from observational records, so hidden differences between patients could bias it. A non-significant difference is not proof of equivalence. The finding is a hypothesis for clinical trials, not grounds to reduce treatment.

articles.headline: The transformer revisited: attention as a soft dictionary lookup
articles.dek: Every token asks a question, compares it against labels on every other token, and takes a weighted blend of what they hold.
body: Start with the problem. A token is one chunk of input, such as a word piece. Before the transformer, models read tokens one at a time with a recurrent neural network (RNN), a network that carries a fixed-size memory forward from step to step. That memory is a bottleneck, because a whole sentence must be squeezed into one vector. Early details fade as the sequence grows. Training is also slow, because step 50 cannot start until step 49 finishes. We want every token to reach every other token directly, and we want the work to run in parallel.

Now the intuition. Picture a Python dictionary: you hand it a lookup string, it finds the matching label, and it returns the stored item. Attention does the same thing, but softly. Imagine asking a room of experts a question. Each expert wears a badge, and each holds a note. You compare your question to every badge, then blend the notes, giving more weight to experts whose badges match well. The analogy breaks in three places. A real dictionary returns exactly one entry, while attention returns a blend. Real dictionary keys are fixed, while here the questions, badges, and notes are all computed from the input by learned matrices (grids of numbers adjusted during training). And the "room" is just the other tokens in the same sequence, not a separate database.

Now the vocabulary. An embedding is a vector (a list of numbers) that represents a token. A query is a vector saying what this token is looking for. A key is a vector advertising what another token offers. A value is a vector holding the content that token will contribute. A dot product multiplies two vectors entry by entry and sums the results, so it is large when they point the same way. A score is the dot product of one query with one key, a raw measure of match. Softmax turns a list of scores into positive numbers that sum to 1, by exponentiating each and dividing by the total. Those outputs are the weights, the fractions of each value that go into the blend.

Here is a tiny example you can check by hand. One query attends over three tokens. The query is \(q=(2,0)\). The keys are \(k_1=(1,0)\), \(k_2=(0,1)\), \(k_3=(1,1)\). The values are \(v_1=(1,2)\), \(v_2=(3,0)\), \(v_3=(0,4)\). Step 1, raw scores: \(q\cdot k_1=2\), \(q\cdot k_2=0\), \(q\cdot k_3=2\). Step 2, divide by \(\sqrt{2}\approx1.41\), because the vectors have 2 dimensions. The scaled scores are 1.41, 0, 1.41. Step 3, exponentiate: 4.11, 1.00, 4.11, which sum to 9.23. Step 4, divide: the weights are about 0.4458, 0.1084, 0.4458. Rounded to two places they are 0.45, 0.11, 0.45, which add to 1.01 only through rounding. Step 5, blend the values using the weights: x = 0.4458·1 + 0.1084·3 + 0.4458·0 = 0.77, and y = 0.4458·2 + 0.1084·0 + 0.4458·4 = 2.67. The output is (0.77, 2.67).
Now the general math. Stack all queries, keys, and values into matrices and compute everything at once:
\[\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

This compares every query to every key, turns each row of scores into weights, and returns one blended value vector per query. Here \(Q\) has shape \(n\times d_k\), with one query per row for \(n\) tokens. \(K\) has shape \(m\times d_k\), with one key per row for \(m\) tokens being looked at, and \(K^{\top}\) is \(K\) with rows and columns swapped. \(V\) has shape \(m\times d_v\), with one value per row. \(d_k\) is the key dimension, and dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps scores from growing with dimension and saturating the softmax. \(d_v\) is the value dimension. The softmax acts on each row separately. The output has shape \(n\times d_v\). In a transformer, \(Q=XW_Q\), \(K=XW_K\), \(V=XW_V\), where \(X\) (shape \(n\times d_{model}\)) holds the token embeddings, \(d_{model}\) is the embedding size, and \(W_Q\), \(W_K\), \(W_V\) are learned projection matrices of shapes \(d_{model}\times d_k\), \(d_{model}\times d_k\), and \(d_{model}\times d_v\). In the example, \(n=1\), \(m=3\), and \(d_k=d_v=2\). The score matrix has \(n\times m\) entries, so cost grows quadratically with sequence length.

Some common confusions. Attention weights are not a learned table of fixed links between positions. They are recomputed from content for every input. The weights are also not a full explanation of why a model said something. Keys and values are different vectors, so what a token advertises can differ from what it gives. Scaling is not cosmetic: without it, large dimensions push softmax toward a hard one-hot choice (all weight on one entry), where gradients, the signals that tell training how to adjust the model, become tiny. Finally, attention alone has no sense of order. Position must be injected separately, since shuffling the keys and values together leaves the blend unchanged.

This is still the core of today's frontier models, such as GPT-style models (generative pre-trained transformers, which generate text one token at a time) and Llama-style models (a family of language models), including open-weight ones whose trained parameters are published. Because of the quadratic cost, the details have changed. Many models use grouped-query attention (GQA), where several query heads (independent copies of attention running side by side) share one set of keys and values. This shrinks the key-value cache, the stored keys and values of earlier tokens that avoid recomputation during generation. Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) encode order by rotating queries and keys. FlashAttention is a GPU program (a kernel) that computes the same result faster by avoiding writes of the full score matrix to memory. Some models also mix in sliding-window layers, where each token looks only at nearby tokens.
articles.why: Nearly every current language, vision, and robotics model is built on this one operation, so its cost and behavior shape what these systems can do.

terms.def: Three vectors computed from each token: what it is looking for, what it advertises, and what content it contributes.
A function that turns a list of scores into positive weights that sum to 1.
Multiply two vectors entry by entry and sum; large when they point in similar directions.
Stored keys and values of earlier tokens, kept during generation so they are not recomputed.
A variant where several query heads share one set of keys and values to save memory.

sources.title: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., 2017)
Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate (Bahdanau et al., 2014)

recap: Attention is a soft dictionary lookup: a query is compared to keys, and the resulting weights blend the values.
The core equation is softmax of scaled query-key dot products, multiplied by the values.
The cost grows with the square of sequence length, which drives most modern attention variants.
deeper: Start with what you need to recall. A token is one chunk of input, such as a word piece. An embedding is a vector, a list of numbers, that represents a token. A dot product multiplies two vectors entry by entry and sums the results, so it is large when they point the same way. Softmax turns a list of raw scores into positive weights that sum to 1.

Now the problem. Before the transformer, models read tokens one at a time with a recurrent neural network (RNN), a network that carries a fixed-size memory forward from step to step. That memory is a bottleneck, because a whole sentence must be squeezed into one vector, and early details fade. Training is also slow, because step 50 cannot start until step 49 finishes. We want every token to reach every other token directly, and we want the work to run in parallel.

Here is the intuition. Picture a Python dictionary: you hand it a lookup string, it finds the matching label, and it returns the stored item. Attention does this softly. Imagine asking a room of experts a question. Each expert wears a badge and holds a note. You compare your question to every badge, then blend the notes, giving more weight to experts whose badges match well. The analogy breaks in three places. A dictionary returns one entry, while attention returns a blend. Dictionary keys are fixed, while here the questions, badges, and notes are computed from the input by learned matrices, which are grids of numbers adjusted during training. And the room is just the other tokens in the same sequence.

The mechanism follows the analogy. A query is a vector saying what a token is looking for. A key is a vector advertising what another token offers. A value is a vector holding the content that token will contribute. Compare one query with each key by dot product to get a score, a raw measure of match. Softmax turns the scores into weights. Then add up the values, each multiplied by its weight.
For one query, the weight on token \(i\) is
\[w_i=\frac{\exp(s_i)}{\sum_j \exp(s_j)}\]

This exponentiates each score and divides by the total, so the weights are positive and sum to 1. Here \(s_i\) is the scaled score for token \(i\), \(\exp\) is the exponential function, and \(j\) runs over all tokens being looked at.
Stacking everything into matrices gives the full operation:
\[\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

This compares every query to every key, turns each row of scores into weights, and returns one blended value vector per query. \(Q\) has shape \(n\times d_k\), one query per row for \(n\) tokens. \(K\) has shape \(m\times d_k\), one key per row for the \(m\) tokens being looked at, and \(K^{\top}\) swaps its rows and columns. \(V\) has shape \(m\times d_v\), one value per row. The symbol \(d_k\) is the key dimension and \(d_v\) is the value dimension. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) keeps scores from growing with dimension. The softmax acts on each row separately, and the output has shape \(n\times d_v\).
The three inputs come from the token embeddings:
\[Q=XW_Q,\quad K=XW_K,\quad V=XW_V\]

Each token's embedding is projected three ways, so one token can advertise one thing and give another. \(X\) has shape \(n\times d_{model}\), where \(d_{model}\) is the embedding size. \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) have shape \(d_{model}\times d_k\), and \(W_V\) has shape \(d_{model}\times d_v\). All three are learned.

Now a check by hand, with \(n=1\), \(m=3\), \(d_k=d_v=2\). Let \(q=(2,0)\), keys \(k_1=(1,0)\), \(k_2=(0,1)\), \(k_3=(1,1)\), and values \(v_1=(1,2)\), \(v_2=(3,0)\), \(v_3=(0,4)\). The raw scores are 2, 0, 2. Dividing by \(\sqrt{2}\approx1.41\) gives 1.41, 0, 1.41. Exponentiating gives 4.11, 1.00, 4.11, which sum to 9.23. The weights are about 0.4458, 0.1084, 0.4458. Rounded to 0.45, 0.11, 0.45 they add to 1.01 only through rounding. The first output entry is \(0.4458\cdot1+0.1084\cdot3+0.4458\cdot0=0.77\). The second is \(0.4458\cdot2+0.1084\cdot0+0.4458\cdot4=2.67\). The output is (0.77, 2.67). Tokens 1 and 3 matched equally well, so they dominate.

Compared with an RNN, every token reaches every other in one step, and all rows compute at once on parallel hardware. The price is that the score matrix has \(n\times m\) entries, so cost grows quadratically with sequence length.

That cost shapes today's designs. Grouped-query attention (GQA) lets several query heads, independent copies of attention running side by side, share one set of keys and values. This shrinks the key-value cache, which stores earlier tokens' keys and values so generation does not recompute them. FlashAttention, a graphics processing unit (GPU) program that computes the same result without writing the full score matrix to memory, makes it faster. Some models add sliding-window layers, where each token sees only nearby tokens.

Some cautions remain. Attention alone has no sense of order, because shuffling keys and values together leaves the blend unchanged. Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) fix this by rotating queries and keys to encode position. The weights are recomputed from content for every input, and they are not a full explanation of a model's output. Without scaling, large dimensions push softmax toward one-hot, with all weight on one entry. Gradients, the signals that tell training how to adjust the model, then become tiny.

articles.headline: Memory as a Ball Rolling Downhill: The Hopfield Network
articles.dek: In 1982, John Hopfield showed that a simple network of on-off units can store memories and repair damaged ones, by treating recall as settling into the bottom of an energy valley.
body: The problem: computers retrieve data by address, so you must know where something is stored. Brains seem to retrieve by content. A smell, a half-heard tune or a smudged face brings back the whole memory. Memory that works this way is called content-addressable memory: you look things up by a piece of the content, not by a location. In 1982 Hopfield, in "Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities" (published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, PNAS, a US science journal), asked whether a crowd of very simple units could produce this behavior collectively, without any central controller.

The intuition: picture a stretched rubber sheet with a few deep dents. Drop a marble anywhere and it rolls into the nearest dent and stops. Each dent is a stored memory. A corrupted memory is a marble that starts partway up a slope. Recall is just rolling downhill. The designer's job is to shape the sheet so the dents sit exactly where the memories are.

The vocabulary. A neuron here is a unit whose state \(s_i\) is either +1 or −1. The network's state is the vector of all such values. A pattern is a state we want to remember. Weights are numbers on the connections between units. An energy function assigns one number to every state, and low energy means a stable state. An attractor is a state that nearby states flow into. A Hopfield network is a set of fully connected neurons, with symmetric weights (the weight from unit i to unit j equals the weight from j to i) and no self-connections, whose attractors are the stored patterns.

The mechanism has two parts. Storing uses the Hebbian rule, "neurons that fire together wire together":
\[ W_{ij} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{\mu=1}^{P} \xi_i^{\mu} \xi_j^{\mu}, \quad W_{ii}=0 \]\nThis makes two units attract each other if they agree across the stored patterns, and repel if they disagree. Here \(W_{ij}\) is the weight between units \(i\) and \(j\) (an \(N\times N\) symmetric matrix), \(N\) is the number of neurons, \(P\) is the number of stored patterns, \(\mu\) is the index that runs over the stored patterns, and \(\xi_i^{\mu}\) is the ±1 value of unit \(i\) in pattern \(\mu\). The factor \(1/N\) just keeps the weights small. Recalling updates one randomly chosen neuron at a time:
\[ s_i \leftarrow \operatorname{sign}\Big(\sum_{j} W_{ij}\, s_j\Big) \]\nEach neuron adopts the sign of the weighted vote of the others. Here \(s_i\) is the state of the neuron being updated, \(s_j\) is the current state of unit \(j\), the sum runs over all units \(j\), and sign returns +1 for positive input and −1 for negative (if the input is exactly zero, the neuron simply keeps its current state).

Why does this converge? Hopfield defined an energy:
\[ E(s) = -\tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i \neq j} W_{ij}\, s_i s_j \]\nThis scores how well the state agrees with the weights, so aligned pairs lower the energy. Here \(E\) is a single number for the whole state \(s\), \(s_i\) and \(s_j\) are neuron states, and the sum runs over all ordered pairs of different neurons, so each pair is counted twice, which the factor \(\tfrac12\) cancels. Because the weights are symmetric, each single-neuron update can only lower \(E\) or leave it unchanged. The energy is bounded below, so the network must stop at a stable state, which is a local minimum, meaning a state where no single flip lowers the energy further.

A tiny example with \(N=4\) and one pattern \(\xi=(+1,+1,-1,-1)\). The rule gives \(W_{12}=W_{34}=+1/4\) and the other four off-diagonal pairs equal −1/4. Corrupt the first bit to get \(s=(-1,+1,-1,-1)\). Neuron 1 receives \(\tfrac14(+1) + (-\tfrac14)(-1) + (-\tfrac14)(-1) = \tfrac34\). That is positive, so it flips to +1 and the pattern is restored. The energy falls from 0 to −1.5, a change of −1.5, which equals \(-\Delta s_1 \cdot \tfrac34\) with \(\Delta s_1=2\) (the change in neuron 1's state, from −1 to +1). The other neurons already agree with the pattern and stay put.

What changed afterward: the model has limits. Capacity grows only in proportion to \(N\), and overloaded networks form false "spurious" memories, stable states that match no stored pattern. Yet the picture of computation as energy minimization, with content-addressable memory as a built-in feature, shaped later energy-based models (models that score each configuration with an energy and prefer low values) and Boltzmann-style networks (networks whose units switch on and off randomly, guided by an energy). Later variants with sharper energy functions store far more patterns, and their retrieval step resembles attention in transformers, where a query softly selects the most similar stored items. Here attention is the operation that lets a model weigh stored items by how well they match a query, and a transformer is a neural network built around attention. The rubber-sheet idea is still there, in new forms.
articles.why: It introduced the idea of memory as stable states of an energy landscape, a framing that still guides how we think about retrieval and associative computation in modern models.

terms.def: A stable state that nearby states flow into under the network's update rule; in a Hopfield network each stored memory is one.
A function that assigns one number to every network state, where lower values mean more stable states; the update rule always moves downhill on it.
A learning rule that strengthens the connection between two units when they are active together across patterns, summarized as 'fire together, wire together'.

recap: A Hopfield network stores patterns in symmetric weights using a Hebbian rule.
Recall means updating neurons one at a time, which can only lower the energy, until the state settles in a stored pattern.
Memory as energy minimization still echoes in energy-based models and attention-like retrieval.
deeper: Start with two reminders. A vector is an ordered list of numbers, and a matrix is a grid of numbers. A local minimum of a function is a point where every small step makes the value rise or stay the same.

Ordinary computer memory is address-based. You must know where an item is stored to fetch it. Brains seem to work by content: a half-heard tune brings back the whole song. This is called content-addressable memory, where a fragment of the content is the lookup key. In 1982, J. J. Hopfield, in "Neural networks and physical systems with emergent collective computational abilities" (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences), asked whether many very simple units could do this collectively, with no central controller.

Picture a stretched rubber sheet with a few deep dents. A marble dropped anywhere rolls into the nearest dent and stops. Each dent is a stored memory. A corrupted memory is a marble that starts partway up a slope, and recall is the roll downhill. The designer's job is to place the dents where the memories are.

Now the mechanism. Each neuron is a unit whose state is +1 or −1. The network's state is the vector of all neuron states. A pattern is a state we want to remember. Every pair of neurons is joined by a weight, a number saying how strongly one unit pushes the other. Weights are symmetric, and no neuron connects to itself.
Storing uses the Hebbian rule, "neurons that fire together wire together":
\[ W_{ij} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{\mu=1}^{P} \xi_i^{\mu} \xi_j^{\mu}, \quad W_{ii}=0 \]

Two units that agree across the stored patterns get a positive weight and attract each other. Units that disagree get a negative weight and repel. Here \(W_{ij}\) is the weight between units \(i\) and \(j\), an \(N\times N\) symmetric matrix. \(N\) is the number of neurons, and \(P\) is the number of stored patterns. The index \(\mu\) runs over patterns, and \(\xi_i^{\mu}\) is the ±1 value of unit \(i\) in pattern \(\mu\). The factor \(1/N\) keeps the weights small.
Recall updates one randomly chosen neuron at a time:
\[ s_i \leftarrow \operatorname{sign}\Big(\sum_{j} W_{ij}\, s_j\Big) \]

Each neuron adopts the sign of the weighted vote of the others. Here \(s_i\) is the neuron being updated, and \(s_j\) is the current state of unit \(j\). The sum runs over all units \(j\). The function sign returns +1 for positive input and −1 for negative input. If the input is exactly zero, the neuron keeps its current state.
Why does this settle down? Hopfield defined an energy, a single number assigned to every state, where low means stable:
\[ E(s) = -\tfrac{1}{2} \sum_{i \neq j} W_{ij}\, s_i s_j \]

This scores how well a state agrees with the weights, so aligned pairs lower the energy. \(E\) is one number for the whole state \(s\). The symbols \(s_i\) and \(s_j\) are neuron states. The sum covers all ordered pairs of different neurons, so each pair appears twice, and the \(\tfrac12\) cancels that. Because the weights are symmetric, each single-neuron update can only lower \(E\) or leave it unchanged. Energy has a lowest possible value, so the dynamics must stop. The stopping point is an attractor, a state that nearby states flow into.

A small example makes this concrete. Take \(N=4\) and one pattern \(\xi=(+1,+1,-1,-1)\). The rule gives \(W_{12}=W_{34}=+\tfrac14\), and the other four off-diagonal weights equal \(-\tfrac14\). Corrupt the first bit to get \(s=(-1,+1,-1,-1)\). Neuron 1 receives
\[ \tfrac14(+1) + \left(-\tfrac14\right)(-1) + \left(-\tfrac14\right)(-1) = \tfrac34. \]

That is positive, so neuron 1 flips to +1 and the pattern is restored. The energy falls from 0 to −1.5. This matches \(-\Delta s_1 \cdot \tfrac34\), where \(\Delta s_1 = 2\) is the change in neuron 1's state, from −1 to +1. The other neurons already agree with the pattern and stay put.

Compared with address-based lookup, the difference is robustness. A conventional table needs an exact key, and one wrong bit finds nothing. Here the stored information is spread across all the weights, and a damaged cue still lands in the right basin, the region of states that roll into one dent. No unit holds a memory alone, and no controller does the searching.

The model has clear limits. Capacity grows only in proportion to \(N\). Overloaded networks form spurious memories, which are stable states matching no stored pattern. Retrieval also finds only a local minimum, not necessarily the best match.

Still, the view of computation as energy minimization, with content-addressable memory built in, shaped later work. Energy-based models score each configuration with an energy and prefer low values. Boltzmann-style networks have units that switch on and off randomly, guided by an energy. Later variants with sharper energy functions store far more patterns. Their retrieval step resembles attention, the operation that weighs stored items by how well they match a query. Transformers are neural networks built around attention. The rubber-sheet idea survives in new forms.
